name: Mississippi

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Mississippi became the 20th state on December 10, 1817. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, Mississippi kept 1 seat in the House. It elected its one member statewide (at-large).

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 23rd through 29th Congresses (1833–1847), Mississippi elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district. This continued after the Apportionment Act of 1842 required districts, and the House seated the members anyway.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 2 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 4 to 5 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 33rd Congress (1853–1855), Mississippi elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Mississippi kept 5 seats in the House.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 5 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 6 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Mississippi kept 7 seats in the House.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Mississippi's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Mississippi kept 8 seats in the House.

events.title: Wood v. Broom
events.text: The Supreme Court held that the 1929 apportionment law had dropped the earlier federal requirements that districts be compact, contiguous and equal in population.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Mississippi's House delegation shrank from 8 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Mississippi kept 7 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Mississippi's House delegation shrank from 7 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Mississippi's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Mississippi kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Mississippi kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Jordan v. Winter
events.text: After Congress amended the Voting Rights Act in 1982, a federal court found its own interim plan diluted Black voting strength and redrew the Delta-based 2nd District with a 52.83% Black voting-age majority. The Supreme Court affirmed in November 1984.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Mississippi kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Mississippi's House delegation shrank from 5 to 4 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Branch v. Smith
events.text: After Mississippi fell to four seats, a state court's plan was not precleared in time, so a federal court imposed its own plan for 2002. In March 2003 the Supreme Court upheld this and said courts, like legislatures, must draw single-member districts.

events.title: Federal court redraws map again
events.text: When the legislature again did not pass a congressional plan, the same federal court amended its earlier judgment and drew new districts on December 30, 2011.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Mississippi kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Mississippi kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c030.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1846 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c034.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which raised Mississippi's seats from 4 to 5. It was first used in the 1854 election.

c035.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1856 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c043.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised Mississippi's seats from 5 to 6. It was first used in the 1872 election.

c045.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1876 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c046.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1878 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c048.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised Mississippi's seats from 6 to 7. It was first used in the 1882 election.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which raised Mississippi's seats from 7 to 8. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which cut Mississippi's seats from 8 to 7. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which cut Mississippi's seats from 7 to 6. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c085.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1956 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which cut Mississippi's seats from 6 to 5. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c090.text: Mississippi's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1966 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left Mississippi with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which left Mississippi with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c099.text: New map following: Jordan v. Winter. After Congress amended the Voting Rights Act in 1982, a federal court found its own interim plan diluted Black voting strength and redrew the Delta-based 2nd District with a 52.83% Black voting-age majority. The Supreme Court affirmed in November 1984.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Mississippi with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map following: Branch v. Smith. After Mississippi fell to four seats, a state court's plan was not precleared in time, so a federal court imposed its own plan for 2002. In March 2003 the Supreme Court upheld this and said courts, like legislatures, must draw single-member districts.

c113.text: New map following: Federal court redraws map again. When the legislature again did not pass a congressional plan, the same federal court amended its earlier judgment and drew new districts on December 30, 2011.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which left Mississippi with 4 seats. It was first used in the 2022 election.
